title: Plan Reading & Tuning — Junior Teaching Track
description: A 10-exercise TEACHING track that introduces PySpark Junior engineers to reading execution plans from scratch. Meet df.explain(), learn the four Catalyst phases, name the six core physical operators, recognize predicate pushdown, the partial+final HashAggregate combiner, and read a 30-line join+aggregate plan. Five modules: PRJ1 What Is a Plan? · PRJ2 The Six Operators · PRJ3 Predicate Pushdown · PRJ4 Two Aggregation Stages · PRJ5 Reading a Real Plan. Companion to PS5–PS7 / PSI1.

datasets.description: Schema reference (sample rows). Junior plan-reading scenarios describe NordGrid Energy at junior scale (500K meters across 4 regions, 200 substations, single cluster).
Substations reference. Used in broadcast-eligible join examples in PRJ5.

tasks.title: What df.explain() Actually Prints

description.context: When a NordGrid junior engineer wants to understand what Spark is actually doing with their code, they call df.explain() — a method that prints Spark's execution plan. There are two common ways to call it: df.explain() prints ONLY the physical plan (what Spark will run), and df.explain(True) prints all four phases (Parsed, Analyzed, Optimized, and Physical) so the engineer can see how Catalyst rewrote the query at each step. Junior engineers usually want only the physical plan because that is what runs.
description.task: Which output is from .explain() and which is from .explain(True)?

evidence.title: Input sample
evidence.content:
Code Called First: meters.filter(col('daily_kw') > 100).explain()

Code Called Second: meters.filter(col('daily_kw') > 100).explain(True)

evidence.title: Dataset
evidence.content: Two output samples from the same query — one called with .explain(), one with .explain(True)

evidence.label: Output A
evidence.content:
== Physical Plan ==
*(1) Filter (isnotnull(daily_kw#3) AND (daily_kw#3 > 100.0))
+- *(1) ColumnarToRow
   +- FileScan parquet [meter_id#0,daily_kw#3]

evidence.label: Output B
evidence.content:
== Parsed Logical Plan ==
'Filter ('daily_kw > 100)
+- 'UnresolvedRelation [meters]

== Analyzed Logical Plan ==
meter_id: string, daily_kw: double
Filter (daily_kw#3 > 100.0)
+- Relation [meter_id#0,daily_kw#3] parquet

== Optimized Logical Plan ==
Filter (isnotnull(daily_kw#3) AND (daily_kw#3 > 100.0))
+- Relation [meter_id#0,daily_kw#3] parquet

== Physical Plan ==
*(1) Filter (isnotnull(daily_kw#3) AND (daily_kw#3 > 100.0))
+- *(1) ColumnarToRow
   +- FileScan parquet [meter_id#0,daily_kw#3]

fields.label: Which output is from .explain() and which is from .explain(True)?
options: A is .explain() — physical plan only. B is .explain(True) — all four phases including Parsed, Analyzed, Optimized, and Physical.
Both are .explain() output; the difference is that B was called on a more complex query that triggered more Catalyst rewrites and so produced more output.
A is .explain(True). B is .explain(). True turns OFF the verbose phase-by-phase output and prints only the compact physical-plan summary.
A is .explain(extended=False) and B is .explain(extended=True). The True/False parameter for explain() is named 'extended', not used positionally.
fields.correctAnswer: A is .explain() — physical plan only. B is .explain(True) — all four phases including Parsed, Analyzed, Optimized, and Physical.
fields.rationale: Output A has only one section header (== Physical Plan ==), so it came from .explain() with no argument. Output B has four section headers (Parsed, Analyzed, Optimized, Physical), so it came from .explain(True). The two are produced from the same query — the only difference is how much detail the engineer asked for. For most junior debugging the physical plan is enough; .explain(True) is reserved for the rare case when the engineer suspects Catalyst is rewriting the query in an unexpected way.
fields.distractorRationale:
Option B: Treats explain output as query-complexity-driven. Output structure depends on the explain mode, not query complexity.

Option C: Reverses the meaning of the True argument. True means MORE output, not less.

Option D: Names a real but rarely-used keyword form; the issue is which output corresponds to which call, not parameter naming.

tasks.pssReference: PS1 lesson 7 (Why Spark Exists — the optimizer's role), PSI1 lesson 2 (The Four Plan Phases — preview at Junior level).

tasks.title: Parsed vs Analyzed vs Optimized vs Physical

description.context: When .explain(True) prints all four phases, each phase represents a stage in Catalyst's optimization journey. The Parsed Logical Plan is what Spark first understood from your code (column names may show as unresolved). The Analyzed Logical Plan resolves column references against the actual schema (so column types appear). The Optimized Logical Plan is what Catalyst rewrote — adding pushdown predicates, removing dead columns, folding constants. The Physical Plan is what Spark will actually run, with concrete operators like FileScan, Filter, and Exchange.

evidence.title: Input sample
evidence.content: Code: meters.filter(col('region') == 'NORTH').select('meter_id').explain(True)

evidence.title: Dataset
evidence.content: Four plan excerpts shuffled out of order; identify which is which phase

evidence.label: Plan output
evidence.content:
Excerpt W:
  Project [meter_id#0]
  +- Filter (isnotnull(region#5) AND (region#5 = NORTH))
     +- Relation [meter_id#0,region#5] parquet

Excerpt X:
  *(1) Project [meter_id#0]
  +- *(1) Filter (isnotnull(region#5) AND (region#5 = NORTH))
     +- *(1) ColumnarToRow
        +- FileScan parquet [meter_id#0,region#5] PushedFilters: [IsNotNull(region), EqualTo(region,NORTH)]

Excerpt Y:
  meter_id: string
  Project [meter_id#0]
  +- Filter (region#5 = NORTH)
     +- Relation [meter_id#0,region#5] parquet

Excerpt Z:
  'Project ['meter_id]
  +- 'Filter ('region = NORTH)
     +- 'UnresolvedRelation [meters]

fields.label: Which excerpt is which phase?
options: W=Parsed, X=Analyzed, Y=Optimized, Z=Physical. Order follows alphabetical letter assignment to phase order in the standard Spark printout.
All four are the same plan printed at different verbosity settings; quote marks and the # numbering change but the underlying tree structure is identical across all phases.
X=Parsed, W=Analyzed, Z=Optimized, Y=Physical. Excerpts go in reverse order from the printed output, so X (with FileScan) is actually the parsed phase.
Z is Parsed because UnresolvedRelation appears. Y is Analyzed because types appear. W is Optimized because IsNotNull was added. X is Physical because FileScan appears.
fields.correctAnswer: Z is Parsed because UnresolvedRelation appears. Y is Analyzed because types appear. W is Optimized because IsNotNull was added. X is Physical because FileScan appears.
fields.rationale: Z is Parsed: 'UnresolvedRelation' and quoted columns ('meter_id) mean Spark has not yet matched names to the schema. Y is Analyzed: column types (meter_id: string) and # numbering appear because Catalyst resolved against the actual table. W is Optimized: the IsNotNull(region) predicate was ADDED by Catalyst (it was not in the original code) — that is the optimizer working. X is Physical: FileScan, ColumnarToRow, and PushedFilters are physical operators with execution-time markers (the *(1) is the codegen stage number).
fields.distractorRationale:
Option A: Assigns phases by letter order; the actual mapping is identifiable from content markers.

Option B: Treats the four phases as the same plan. Each phase represents a different Catalyst stage.

Option C: Reverses order without checking the markers (UnresolvedRelation, types, PushedFilters).

tasks.pssReference: PSI1 lesson 2 (The Four Plan Phases — preview at Junior level).

tasks.title: FileScan, Filter, Project — The First Three

description.context: Three of the most common operators in any physical plan are FileScan, Filter, and Project. FileScan is the line that says 'read these columns from these files on disk'. Filter is the line that narrows ROWS — only those matching a condition pass through. Project is the line that narrows COLUMNS — only the listed columns continue. Physical plans read BOTTOM-TO-TOP: the bottom operator runs first, then its result flows up to the next operator. So a plan with FileScan at the bottom, Filter in the middle, and Project at the top means Spark scans first, filters next, projects last.
description.task: What does Spark do FIRST when running this plan?

evidence.title: Input sample
evidence.content: Code: meters.filter(col('daily_kw') > 100).select('meter_id', 'daily_kw').explain()

evidence.title: Dataset
evidence.content: Minimal 4-line plan with FileScan, Filter, and Project — student labels each operator and confirms execution order

evidence.label: Plan output
evidence.content:
== Physical Plan ==
*(1) Project [meter_id#0, daily_kw#3]
+- *(1) Filter (isnotnull(daily_kw#3) AND (daily_kw#3 > 100.0))
   +- *(1) ColumnarToRow
      +- FileScan parquet [meter_id#0,daily_kw#3] PushedFilters: [IsNotNull(daily_kw), GreaterThan(daily_kw,100.0)]

fields.label: What does Spark do FIRST when running this plan?
options: Project — Spark first chooses which columns to keep (meter_id, daily_kw). The Project line is at the top of the plan, and physical plans run top-to-bottom.
Filter — Spark first applies the filter condition daily_kw > 100. The filter is between Project and FileScan in the plan, and runs before either.
FileScan — Spark first reads the columns from the parquet files. FileScan is the bottom operator in the plan, and physical plans run bottom-to-top.
ColumnarToRow — Spark first converts columnar parquet format into row format because all subsequent operators need row-style data. ColumnarToRow runs before FileScan.
fields.correctAnswer: FileScan — Spark first reads the columns from the parquet files. FileScan is the bottom operator in the plan, and physical plans run bottom-to-top.
fields.rationale: Physical plans read bottom-to-top: the operator at the bottom runs first, and its output flows up. FileScan is at the bottom, so Spark reads the parquet files first (with the pushed-down predicates already applied). The data then flows up through ColumnarToRow (format conversion), then Filter (any conditions not pushed down), then Project (narrow to the requested columns). The visual order in the plan output is the reverse of execution order — that is the most common Junior confusion when first reading plans.
fields.distractorRationale:
Option A: Reads physical plans top-to-bottom; they execute bottom-to-top.

Option B: Picks the middle operator without applying the bottom-to-top rule.

Option D: Confuses ColumnarToRow position; it sits between FileScan and Filter and runs second, not first.

tasks.pssReference: PSI1 lesson 3 (Reading Physical Plans — bottom-to-top conventions).

tasks.title: Exchange Means Shuffle

description.context: Exchange is the operator name Spark uses for a SHUFFLE — moving rows between executors. When data needs to be redistributed (because a groupBy needs all rows with the same key on the same executor, or a join needs matching keys co-located), Spark inserts an Exchange operator in the plan. The most common form is Exchange hashpartitioning(column, N) — meaning Spark hashes that column and sends each row to one of N partitions. Other forms exist (Exchange RangePartitioning for sorts, Exchange RoundRobinPartitioning for balanced repartitioning) but hash partitioning is the one Junior engineers see most often.
description.task: What does the Exchange line tell you about what Spark is doing?

evidence.title: Input sample
evidence.content: Code: meters.groupBy('region').agg(sum('daily_kw').alias('total')).explain()

evidence.title: Dataset
evidence.content: Plan with one Exchange hashpartitioning operator visible from a groupBy

evidence.label: Plan output
evidence.content:
== Physical Plan ==
AdaptiveSparkPlan isFinalPlan=false
+- HashAggregate(keys=[region#5], functions=[sum(daily_kw#3)])
   +- Exchange hashpartitioning(region#5, 200), [plan_id=14]
      +- HashAggregate(keys=[region#5], functions=[partial_sum(daily_kw#3)])
         +- FileScan parquet [region#5,daily_kw#3]

fields.label: What does the Exchange line tell you about what Spark is doing?
options: Spark is sorting the data by region before aggregating; Exchange means a sort step takes place. The number 200 is how many sort buffers Spark will use.
Spark is shuffling by hashing region into 200 partitions; rows with the same region land on the same executor so HashAggregate above can sum them. Exchange means shuffle.
Exchange is an internal Spark operator that does not affect runtime; it is a placeholder Catalyst inserts during planning that disappears at execution time.
Spark is doing data exchange between the driver and executors; the 200 means 200 rows are sent at a time. This is how Spark transmits results to the application from worker nodes.
fields.correctAnswer: Spark is shuffling by hashing region into 200 partitions; rows with the same region land on the same executor so HashAggregate above can sum them. Exchange means shuffle.
fields.rationale: Exchange is the physical-plan name for a SHUFFLE — redistributing rows across executors. hashpartitioning(region#5, 200) means Spark hashes the region column and sends each row to one of 200 partitions; rows with the same hash land on the same executor. This is necessary for the HashAggregate above the Exchange to sum all rows for each region (it needs them co-located). The 200 is spark.sql.shuffle.partitions default. Exchange ALWAYS means a shuffle, regardless of which partitioning form follows.
fields.distractorRationale:
Option A: Confuses Exchange with Sort. Exchange is movement; Sort is ordering. Different operators.

Option C: Treats Exchange as an inert placeholder; it is the actual shuffle step at runtime.

Option D: Confuses executor-to-executor shuffle with driver-to-executor result transmission. Exchange is between executors.

tasks.pssReference: PSI1 lesson 3 (Reading Physical Plans — Exchange as shuffle).

description.context: When you write a filter like .filter(col('daily_kw') > 100), you might expect Spark to load every row and then check the condition. It usually does something smarter: it tells the file reader to skip rows that fail the condition BEFORE they enter Spark's memory. This optimization is called PREDICATE PUSHDOWN. In a physical plan, look at the FileScan line for a field called PushedFilters: [...]. Filter conditions that pushed down appear in this list. Conditions that did NOT push down stay as a separate Filter operator above the FileScan. Pushdown matters because it can reduce data read from disk by 100× or more.
description.task: Which condition pushed down to the file reader, and which did not?

evidence.title: Input sample
evidence.content: Code: meters.filter((col('daily_kw') > 100) & (col('region') == 'NORTH')).explain()

evidence.title: Dataset
evidence.content: A physical plan from a NordGrid query with two filter conditions, one pushed down and one not

evidence.label: Plan output
evidence.content:
== Physical Plan ==
*(1) Filter (isnotnull(daily_kw#3) AND (daily_kw#3 > 100.0))
+- *(1) ColumnarToRow
   +- FileScan parquet [meter_id#0,daily_kw#3,region#5]
      PushedFilters: [IsNotNull(region), EqualTo(region,NORTH)]

fields.label: Which condition pushed down to the file reader, and which did not?
options: Both conditions pushed down. The Filter operator above is a leftover that Spark always shows even when filters are fully pushed down to the file reader; safe to ignore.
Neither condition pushed down. PushedFilters: [...] is just a debug label; actual filtering always happens in the Filter operator above the FileScan line.
region == 'NORTH' pushed down (it is in PushedFilters). daily_kw > 100 did NOT push down (it remained as a separate Filter above FileScan). Both happen but at different layers.
daily_kw > 100 pushed down because it is in the Filter operator at the top of the plan. region == 'NORTH' did not push down because it appears below FileScan in the PushedFilters list.
fields.correctAnswer: region == 'NORTH' pushed down (it is in PushedFilters). daily_kw > 100 did NOT push down (it remained as a separate Filter above FileScan). Both happen but at different layers.
fields.rationale: PushedFilters: [IsNotNull(region), EqualTo(region,NORTH)] tells you which conditions the parquet reader applied while loading. region == 'NORTH' is there, so it pushed down — the reader skipped rows for other regions before Spark saw them. daily_kw > 100 is NOT in PushedFilters; instead it appears in the Filter operator at the top of the plan. That means Spark loaded all rows passing the region filter, then applied the daily_kw filter in memory. Reading the plan tells you exactly where each filter is being evaluated.
fields.distractorRationale:
Option A: Treats the residual Filter operator as inert; it is the actual second-stage filter.

Option B: Treats PushedFilters as decorative. It is the authoritative list of file-reader-applied conditions.

Option D: Reverses the meaning of plan position. Filter at top runs LAST; PushedFilters runs at the file reader (first).

tasks.title: Why a UDF Filter Did Not Push Down

description.context: Not every filter can push down. For pushdown to work, Spark needs to express the condition in a form the file reader understands — equality, range comparison, IS NULL, IS NOT NULL, simple boolean combinations. When you wrap a column in a Python UDF (a user-defined function), Spark cannot translate the function call into something the file reader can evaluate. The file reader is a Java/native library; it does not run Python code. So filters using UDFs always stay as a separate Filter operator above the FileScan, and Spark must load every row to evaluate them.
description.task: Why does Plan B's filter not push down, and what is the runtime cost?

evidence.title: Input sample
evidence.content:
Code A: meters.filter(col('daily_kw') > 100).explain()

Code B: is_high = udf(lambda kw: kw > 100, 'boolean')
meters.filter(is_high(col('daily_kw'))).explain()

evidence.title: Dataset
evidence.content: Two side-by-side plans from queries that look similar — one filter pushes down, one does not because of a UDF

evidence.label: Plan A — built-in comparison
evidence.content:
== Physical Plan ==
*(1) Filter (isnotnull(daily_kw#3) AND (daily_kw#3 > 100.0))
+- *(1) ColumnarToRow
   +- FileScan parquet [daily_kw#3]
      PushedFilters: [IsNotNull(daily_kw), GreaterThan(daily_kw,100.0)]

evidence.label: Plan B — UDF wrapping the same condition
evidence.content:
== Physical Plan ==
*(1) Filter pythonUDF0#15: boolean
+- BatchEvalPython [is_high(daily_kw#3)#14], [pythonUDF0#15]
   +- *(1) ColumnarToRow
      +- FileScan parquet [daily_kw#3]
         PushedFilters: []

fields.label: Why does Plan B's filter not push down, and what is the runtime cost?
options: Plan B uses a UDF; Spark cannot translate Python code into a parquet reader predicate. PushedFilters is empty, so the reader returns ALL rows. BatchEvalPython runs the UDF in a Python worker. Cost: full scan plus Python overhead.
Plan B's UDF correctly pushed down — BatchEvalPython is the optimized form of pushdown for Python functions. The empty PushedFilters list is misleading; Spark uses a different mechanism for UDFs.
Plan B's filter pushes down but produces wrong results because the UDF returns Python bool instead of Java Boolean; the cast in BatchEvalPython is a workaround. Cost: small CPU overhead for the cast.
Plan B is functionally identical to Plan A. BatchEvalPython is added by Catalyst even when no Python is involved; PushedFilters is empty because of an unrelated planner bug. Cost: same as Plan A.
fields.correctAnswer: Plan B uses a UDF; Spark cannot translate Python code into a parquet reader predicate. PushedFilters is empty, so the reader returns ALL rows. BatchEvalPython runs the UDF in a Python worker. Cost: full scan plus Python overhead.
fields.rationale: PushedFilters: [] in Plan B is the key signal. The parquet reader applies no filter and returns all rows. BatchEvalPython then runs the UDF on every row in a separate Python worker process with serialization both ways. Plan A's PushedFilters: [IsNotNull(daily_kw), GreaterThan(daily_kw,100.0)] means the reader skips most rows on disk. The two plans look similar in code but differ dramatically at runtime: Plan A reads filtered data; Plan B reads everything plus pays Python serialization cost. Junior engineers should default to built-in functions and reach for UDFs only when no built-in equivalent exists.
fields.distractorRationale:
Option B: Misreads BatchEvalPython as pushdown. It is UDF evaluation AFTER the file is read.

Option C: Invents a casting bug. Python/Java Boolean conversion is automatic.

Option D: Treats the two plans as equivalent. The empty PushedFilters list is the meaningful difference.

tasks.pssReference: PSI1 lesson 4 (Predicate Pushdown — limits with UDFs).

tasks.title: HashAggregate(partial) Above the Exchange

description.context: Every groupBy plan in Spark contains TWO HashAggregate operators, not one. The bottom one — labeled HashAggregate(...partial_sum...) — runs on each executor BEFORE the shuffle. It does a local reduction so each executor only sends its already-summed rows over the network. The top one — labeled HashAggregate(...sum...) — runs AFTER the Exchange and combines the partial results from all executors into the final answer. This pattern is called the COMBINER PATTERN. The partial step dramatically reduces shuffle volume: a 12M-row groupBy with 4 regions sends 4 partial rows per executor instead of millions of raw rows.
description.task: Why does the plan have TWO HashAggregate operators?

evidence.title: Input sample
evidence.content: Code: meters.groupBy('region').agg(sum('daily_kw').alias('total')).explain()

evidence.title: Dataset
evidence.content: A groupBy plan showing the partial+final HashAggregate pattern with Exchange between them

evidence.label: Plan output
evidence.content:
== Physical Plan ==
AdaptiveSparkPlan isFinalPlan=false
+- HashAggregate(keys=[region#5], functions=[sum(daily_kw#3)])
   +- Exchange hashpartitioning(region#5, 200), [plan_id=14]
      +- HashAggregate(keys=[region#5], functions=[partial_sum(daily_kw#3)])
         +- FileScan parquet [region#5,daily_kw#3]

fields.label: Why does the plan have TWO HashAggregate operators?
options: Spark made a mistake; one of the HashAggregate operators is redundant in this plan. The optimizer should have removed it but did not. Performance impact: minor double-work that runs twice.
The bottom one (partial_sum) is incomplete and produces wrong results; the top one (sum) re-runs the aggregation correctly. Spark always retries aggregations to ensure correctness.

The bottom HashAggregate(partial_sum) reduces rows on each executor BEFORE the shuffle, so only summed-per-executor rows cross the network. The top HashAggregate combines the partials. This is the combiner pattern.
The two HashAggregate operators handle different parts of the GROUP BY clause; the bottom handles the keys, the top handles the aggregate function. They are independent steps, not related.
fields.correctAnswer: The bottom HashAggregate(partial_sum) reduces rows on each executor BEFORE the shuffle, so only summed-per-executor rows cross the network. The top HashAggregate combines the partials. This is the combiner pattern.
fields.rationale: The combiner pattern is one of the most important reading skills for groupBy plans. The bottom HashAggregate runs on each executor's local data and produces ONE row per region per executor (the partial sum). Then the Exchange shuffles those small results — 4 regions × N executors instead of 12M raw rows. The top HashAggregate combines the per-executor partials into the final 4-row result. Without the partial step, every row would cross the network. When the partial step is missing (which happens with non-mergeable UDAFs), shuffle volume can be 1000× larger.
fields.distractorRationale:
Option A: Treats the partial as redundant; it is the optimizer's correct optimization.

Option B: Treats the partial as wrong; it produces partial sums that the final step combines correctly.

Option D: Splits the work by clause type. Both operators handle keys+aggregate together; they differ in WHEN they run (per-executor vs post-shuffle).

tasks.pssReference: PSI1 lesson 3 (Reading Physical Plans), JAI3 module (Partial Aggregation in the recognition track).

tasks.title: The Plan Without a Partial Stage

description.context: The partial+final HashAggregate pattern only works when the aggregate function can be split into a partial step and a final step. Built-in aggregates like sum, count, min, max, avg can be split — they are MERGEABLE. But certain user-defined aggregates and some functions like collect_list cannot be split because their accumulator state cannot be merged across partitions. When that happens, Catalyst skips the partial step and produces a plan with only ONE HashAggregate above the Exchange. Every row of input must then shuffle before aggregation. At 12M rows the difference is dramatic.
description.task: What is the key difference between the two plans, and what is the performance impact?

evidence.title: Input sample
evidence.content:
Code A: meters.groupBy('region').agg(sum('daily_kw').alias('total')).explain()

Code B: meters.groupBy('region').agg(collect_list('meter_id').alias('ids')).explain()

evidence.title: Dataset
evidence.content: Two side-by-side plans for similar groupBy queries — one with partial+final, one with only final

evidence.label: Plan A — sum() aggregation
evidence.content:
== Physical Plan ==
AdaptiveSparkPlan isFinalPlan=false
+- HashAggregate(keys=[region#5], functions=[sum(daily_kw#3)])
   +- Exchange hashpartitioning(region#5, 200)
      +- HashAggregate(keys=[region#5], functions=[partial_sum(daily_kw#3)])
         +- FileScan parquet [region#5,daily_kw#3]

evidence.label: Plan B — collect_list() aggregation
evidence.content:
== Physical Plan ==
AdaptiveSparkPlan isFinalPlan=false
+- ObjectHashAggregate(keys=[region#5], functions=[collect_list(meter_id#0)])
   +- Exchange hashpartitioning(region#5, 200)
      +- FileScan parquet [region#5,meter_id#0]

fields.label: What is the key difference between the two plans, and what is the performance impact?
options: Plan B uses ObjectHashAggregate instead of HashAggregate; this is a naming variant for the same operation. No performance difference between the two plans.
Plan B is faster because it has fewer operators; fewer steps means less coordination overhead. Plan A has redundant HashAggregate operators that slow it down considerably.
Plan A has a missing operator — there should be a Sort step before aggregation; this is a Catalyst bug. Plan B is the correctly-optimized form of the query.
Plan A has TWO HashAggregate stages (partial+final). Plan B has only ONE because collect_list cannot split across partitions. Plan B shuffles every input row; Plan A shuffles only summed rows.
fields.correctAnswer: Plan A has TWO HashAggregate stages (partial+final). Plan B has only ONE because collect_list cannot split across partitions. Plan B shuffles every input row; Plan A shuffles only summed rows.
fields.rationale: Plan A has the partial+final pattern with a partial_sum step BEFORE the Exchange, so each executor reduces its local data before shuffling. Plan B has no operator below the Exchange — every row shuffles to its destination executor before aggregation begins. ObjectHashAggregate vs HashAggregate is a minor implementation detail (different state representation); the missing partial step is the major performance difference. At 12M rows × 4 regions, Plan A shuffles ~4 partial rows per executor; Plan B shuffles 12M rows. The pattern recurs whenever an aggregate cannot merge its accumulator across partitions.
fields.distractorRationale:
Option A: Treats ObjectHashAggregate vs HashAggregate as the difference; the missing partial step matters more.

Option B: Counts operators as a performance proxy; fewer operators here means MORE work because the partial reduction is absent.

Option C: Invents a missing-Sort hypothesis. Neither plan needs Sort because the aggregation does not require it.

tasks.pssReference: JAI3 module (Partial Aggregation in recognition track), PSI1 lesson 3 (Reading Physical Plans).

tasks.title: Reading a NordGrid Join+Aggregate Plan

description.context: Time to put it all together. A NordGrid junior engineer wrote a query that joins meter readings with substation reference data and aggregates by region. The senior engineer asks them to read the resulting physical plan and answer four questions about it. Every operator from PRJ2 should be recognizable; the partial+final pattern from PRJ4 should appear; and one new feature shows up for the first time — the BroadcastHashJoin operator, which is what Spark uses when one side of a join is small enough to copy to every executor.
description.task: Read the plan above, then answer the questions in order.

evidence.title: Dataset
evidence.content: A 4-stage physical plan from a meters × substations join with groupBy aggregation

evidence.label: Plan output
evidence.content:
code = (meters
    .filter(col('daily_kw') > 100)
    .join(broadcast(substations), on='substation_id', how='inner')
    .groupBy('region')
    .agg(sum('daily_kw').alias('total_kw'), count('*').alias('n_meters')))
code.explain()

== Physical Plan ==
AdaptiveSparkPlan isFinalPlan=false
+- HashAggregate(keys=[region#22], functions=[sum(daily_kw#3), count(1)])
   +- Exchange hashpartitioning(region#22, 200), [plan_id=58]
      +- HashAggregate(keys=[region#22], functions=[partial_sum(daily_kw#3), partial_count(1)])
         +- Project [daily_kw#3, region#22]
            +- BroadcastHashJoin [substation_id#7], [substation_id#19], Inner, BuildRight
               :- Filter (isnotnull(daily_kw#3) AND (daily_kw#3 > 100.0))
               :  +- ColumnarToRow
               :     +- FileScan parquet [meter_id#0, daily_kw#3, substation_id#7]
               :        PushedFilters: [IsNotNull(daily_kw), GreaterThan(daily_kw,100.0), IsNotNull(substation_id)]
               +- BroadcastExchange HashedRelationBroadcastMode
                  +- Filter isnotnull(substation_id#19)
                     +- FileScan parquet [substation_id#19, region#22]
                        PushedFilters: [IsNotNull(substation_id)]

fields.label: Q1 — How many shuffles does this plan trigger? (A shuffle is an Exchange operator.)
options: Two shuffles. One Exchange line is visible (after partial aggregation), and the BroadcastHashJoin counts as a shuffle because both sides need to redistribute by the join key.
One shuffle. Only one Exchange operator is visible in the plan (between partial and final HashAggregate). BroadcastHashJoin avoids the shuffle that a regular SortMergeJoin would have caused.
Three shuffles. Each FileScan is a shuffle (data movement from disk), the BroadcastExchange is a shuffle, and the Exchange between the HashAggregates is a third shuffle.
Zero shuffles. Catalyst has fully optimized the query and removed all data movement; the plan runs entirely on local executor data without any redistribution.
fields.correctAnswer: One shuffle. Only one Exchange operator is visible in the plan (between partial and final HashAggregate). BroadcastHashJoin avoids the shuffle that a regular SortMergeJoin would have caused.
fields.rationale: Counting Exchange operators is the standard method for shuffle inventory. BroadcastHashJoin sends a copy of the right side to every executor (via BroadcastExchange) but does NOT shuffle either side by the join key — that is the whole point of broadcasting. A regular SortMergeJoin would have required two shuffles (one per side); broadcast eliminates both. So total shuffles in this plan: one.
fields.distractorRationale:
Option A: Counts BroadcastHashJoin as a shuffle; it avoids shuffling, which is its purpose.

Option C: Treats FileScan as a shuffle; FileScan is reading data, not redistributing it.

Option D: Misses the visible Exchange operator entirely.

fields.label: Q2 — Where is the broadcast join visible in the plan, and which side is being broadcast?
options: Broadcasting is invisible in physical plans because it is a runtime decision. The BroadcastHashJoin is just a name — the actual broadcast happens at execution time and is not annotated in the plan.
The first FileScan is the broadcast — Spark broadcasts the meters table because it is filtered to only daily_kw > 100. The substations table is not broadcast; it is scanned normally.

BroadcastHashJoin annotates BuildRight at the operator line, which signals that the smaller table on its right branch becomes the hash table. Below it the BroadcastExchange confirms which input gets copied.
Both sides are broadcast. BroadcastHashJoin always broadcasts both sides to all executors; it is faster than other joins because both sides become local data on every executor.
fields.correctAnswer: BroadcastHashJoin annotates BuildRight at the operator line, which signals that the smaller table on its right branch becomes the hash table. Below it the BroadcastExchange confirms which input gets copied.
fields.rationale: Reading the BuildRight annotation along with the right-branch operator chain identifies the broadcasted input. Below the operator, the right branch shows BroadcastExchange — that is where the actual broadcasting happens. The left branch shows a regular ColumnarToRow + FileScan with no broadcast involvement.
fields.distractorRationale:
Option A: Treats broadcasting as invisible; the BroadcastExchange operator IS the broadcast.

Option B: Reverses which side is broadcast. Filtered does not mean broadcast.

Option D: Treats both sides as broadcast; only one side is broadcast in a BroadcastHashJoin.

fields.label: Q3 — Where is the partial-aggregation step (the combiner pattern), and what does it do?
options: There is no partial step in this plan; the engineer used count(*) which disables partial aggregation. Only the final HashAggregate runs at the top of the plan.
BroadcastHashJoin is the partial step; broadcast joins always include partial aggregation because the right side is small enough to combine on each executor.
The Project operator above BroadcastHashJoin is the partial step; Project narrows columns and that counts as a partial reduction in row size before aggregation.
The HashAggregate(partial_sum, partial_count) below the Exchange. It runs on each executor's joined+filtered data, producing per-region partial results that the Exchange shuffles.
fields.correctAnswer: The HashAggregate(partial_sum, partial_count) below the Exchange. It runs on each executor's joined+filtered data, producing per-region partial results that the Exchange shuffles.
fields.rationale: The HashAggregate with functions=[partial_sum(daily_kw#3), partial_count(1)] is the combiner step. It sits BELOW the Exchange, so it runs on each executor's locally-joined-and-filtered data. Each executor produces a few region-level partials; the Exchange shuffles those small results; the top HashAggregate combines them into the final 4-region answer. Both sum and count are mergeable aggregates, so partial aggregation is enabled.
fields.distractorRationale:
Option A: Claims count(*) disables partial; sum and count are both partial-eligible.

Option B: Conflates broadcast join with partial aggregation; they are independent optimizations.

Option C: Confuses Project (column narrowing) with partial aggregation (row reduction).

fields.label: Q4 — What does PushedFilters: [IsNotNull(daily_kw), GreaterThan(daily_kw,100.0), IsNotNull(substation_id)] tell you?
options: Three conditions pushed down to the parquet reader: daily_kw is not null, daily_kw > 100, and substation_id is not null. The reader skips rows failing these BEFORE Spark sees them.
Three conditions failed to push down; PushedFilters lists conditions Catalyst tried to push but could not. The Filter operator above applied them in memory afterward.
PushedFilters is informational only; the parquet reader does not actually skip rows. Filter conditions always run in Spark's memory regardless of what PushedFilters lists at the FileScan.
Three filters were applied at the broadcast side; broadcast joins push filters into both the broadcast and the main scan. The list shows what filtering happened on substations rather than meters.
fields.correctAnswer: Three conditions pushed down to the parquet reader: daily_kw is not null, daily_kw > 100, and substation_id is not null. The reader skips rows failing these BEFORE Spark sees them.
fields.rationale: PushedFilters lists conditions the parquet reader actually applies while reading. All three conditions are in the list, so the reader skips rows where daily_kw is null, daily_kw <= 100, or substation_id is null — BEFORE handing rows to Spark. This dramatically reduces I/O. The IsNotNull conditions are added by Catalyst automatically; the substation_id IsNotNull is added because the join key cannot be null.
fields.distractorRationale:
Option B: Reverses the meaning of PushedFilters; the list contains pushed conditions, not failed ones.

Option C: Treats PushedFilters as cosmetic; it directly controls what the parquet reader skips.

Option D: Locates the filters on the wrong side; they appear on the meters scan.

tasks.pssReference: PSI1 lessons 3-4 (Reading Physical Plans, Predicate Pushdown), JAI3 (Partial Aggregation).

tasks.title: Same Query, Different Plans

description.context: Final exercise of the Junior track. The same NordGrid query is run twice — once without a broadcast hint and once with broadcast(substations). The two plans look different. The student is asked to compare them and answer four questions about WHAT differs, WHY one is faster, where AQE annotations show up at runtime, and what would change at 100× scale. Every operator from PRJ2-PRJ4 is in play, plus the AdaptiveSparkPlan annotation that shows up in modern Spark.
description.task: Read the plan above, then answer the questions in order.

evidence.title: Dataset
evidence.content: Two physical plans for the same query — Plan A without broadcast hint, Plan B with broadcast hint

evidence.label: Plan output
evidence.content:
# Plan A — no broadcast hint
code_a = (meters
    .join(substations, on='substation_id', how='inner')
    .groupBy('region').agg(sum('daily_kw').alias('total')))
code_a.explain()

== Physical Plan ==
AdaptiveSparkPlan isFinalPlan=false
+- HashAggregate(keys=[region#22], functions=[sum(daily_kw#3)])
   +- Exchange hashpartitioning(region#22, 200)
      +- HashAggregate(keys=[region#22], functions=[partial_sum(daily_kw#3)])
         +- Project [daily_kw#3, region#22]
            +- SortMergeJoin [substation_id#7], [substation_id#19], Inner
               :- Sort [substation_id#7 ASC NULLS FIRST], false
               :  +- Exchange hashpartitioning(substation_id#7, 200)
               :     +- FileScan parquet meters
               +- Sort [substation_id#19 ASC NULLS FIRST], false
                  +- Exchange hashpartitioning(substation_id#19, 200)
                     +- FileScan parquet substations

# Plan B — with broadcast hint
code_b = (meters
    .join(broadcast(substations), on='substation_id', how='inner')
    .groupBy('region').agg(sum('daily_kw').alias('total')))
code_b.explain()

== Physical Plan ==
AdaptiveSparkPlan isFinalPlan=false
+- HashAggregate(keys=[region#22], functions=[sum(daily_kw#3)])
   +- Exchange hashpartitioning(region#22, 200)
      +- HashAggregate(keys=[region#22], functions=[partial_sum(daily_kw#3)])
         +- Project [daily_kw#3, region#22]
            +- BroadcastHashJoin [substation_id#7], [substation_id#19], Inner, BuildRight
               :- FileScan parquet meters
               +- BroadcastExchange HashedRelationBroadcastMode
                  +- FileScan parquet substations

fields.label: Q1 — How many shuffles does each plan trigger?
options: Plan A: 3 shuffles (two for the join sides + one for groupBy). Plan B: 1 shuffle (just the groupBy; broadcast removed both join shuffles entirely).
Both plans have the same number of shuffles. Broadcast hints affect the join algorithm but do not change the number of shuffles in the resulting plan.
Plan A: 1 shuffle. Plan B: 0 shuffles. The broadcast hint eliminates ALL shuffles including the groupBy because rows with the same region also share the same substation.
Plan A: 2 shuffles (one per Exchange visible). Plan B: 2 shuffles (BroadcastExchange + groupBy Exchange both count). Same total shuffle count for both plans.
fields.correctAnswer: Plan A: 3 shuffles (two for the join sides + one for groupBy). Plan B: 1 shuffle (just the groupBy; broadcast removed both join shuffles entirely).
fields.rationale: Plan A has three Exchange operators: one shuffles meters by substation_id, one shuffles substations by substation_id (both for SortMergeJoin), and one shuffles by region for the groupBy. Plan B has only one Exchange (the groupBy one); the BroadcastExchange is technically a different operation — it copies a small side to every executor rather than redistributing both sides. So broadcast eliminates two of the three shuffles. This is the main reason BroadcastHashJoin is faster than SortMergeJoin when the small-side fits.
fields.distractorRationale:
Option B: Treats join algorithm as decoupled from shuffles; it is the central decision.

Option C: Claims broadcast eliminates the groupBy shuffle, which it cannot.

Option D: Treats BroadcastExchange as a regular shuffle; it is a one-way copy, not a redistribution.

fields.label: Q2 — Why is Plan B faster at NordGrid Junior scale (500K meters, 200 substations)?
options: Plan B is NOT faster at this scale; broadcast hints only help when the broadcast side exceeds 10MB. With 200 substations the broadcast overhead exceeds the savings from avoiding shuffles.

Plan B avoids shuffling meters and substations by replicating substations to every executor. Network traffic drops; sort-merge's two Sort+Exchange branches are replaced with one BroadcastExchange of the smaller side.
Plan B is faster because it has fewer total operators in the printed plan; fewer steps means less Catalyst overhead at runtime. The broadcast hint shortcuts the Catalyst planning step.
Plan B is faster because BroadcastHashJoin uses GPU acceleration on modern Spark clusters; SortMergeJoin runs only on CPU and never engages with available GPU resources.
fields.correctAnswer: Plan B avoids shuffling meters and substations by replicating substations to every executor. Network traffic drops; sort-merge's two Sort+Exchange branches are replaced with one BroadcastExchange of the smaller side.
fields.rationale: At any scale where one side is small (200 rows × hundreds of bytes), broadcasting wins. Plan A's two Sort+Exchange branches push every row of meters AND every row of substations across the network and sort both sides. Plan B copies the tiny substations table to every executor once; meters never moves at all for the join. The groupBy Exchange is the same in both. Broadcasting trades a small fixed overhead for eliminating two large shuffles.
fields.distractorRationale:
Option A: Reverses the broadcast use case; broadcast helps when small-side is BELOW the threshold, not above.

Option C: Counts operators as a performance proxy; the actual savings come from avoided shuffles.

Option D: Invents GPU acceleration; not a Spark feature.

fields.label: Q3 — Both plans show AdaptiveSparkPlan isFinalPlan=false at the top. What does this mean?
options: AdaptiveSparkPlan means the plan is invalid and Spark refused to run it; isFinalPlan=false confirms Spark stopped at planning. Re-run the query to get a valid plan that will execute correctly.
AdaptiveSparkPlan is a synonym for the physical plan; isFinalPlan=false is the default value with no operational meaning. Junior engineers should ignore this marker entirely.
Adaptive query execution is disabled; the false flag confirms AQE is off. To enable adaptive optimization, set spark.sql.adaptive.enabled=true in the SparkSession configuration.

The plan was generated by .explain() before execution; isFinalPlan=false means AQE has not yet adapted the plan at runtime. After execution, isFinalPlan=true and any AQE annotations appear in the plan.
fields.correctAnswer: The plan was generated by .explain() before execution; isFinalPlan=false means AQE has not yet adapted the plan at runtime. After execution, isFinalPlan=true and any AQE annotations appear in the plan.
fields.rationale: AdaptiveSparkPlan is the top-level wrapper that AQE uses. isFinalPlan=false means .explain() was called BEFORE the query ran, so AQE has not yet adapted anything. If you call .explain() AFTER an action like .collect() or .count(), isFinalPlan=true and you may see AQEShuffleRead operators showing what AQE actually did at runtime (coalesce, skew split, broadcast conversion). At Junior level you mostly see false because students explore plans before running.
fields.distractorRationale:
Option A: Treats false as an error; it is the normal pre-execution state.

Option B: Dismisses the marker; it is meaningful for distinguishing pre- and post-execution plans.

Option C: Confuses isFinalPlan with adaptive.enabled; AdaptiveSparkPlan only appears when AQE IS enabled.

fields.label: Q4 — At Mid scale (12M meters, the same 200 substations), which plan is preferred?
options: Plan A becomes preferred at 12M meters because shuffling 12M rows is more efficient than broadcasting 200 substations to many executors. Sort-merge scales better with growing data size on the large side.

Plan B remains preferred because the substations table is still tiny; broadcasting it eliminates the 12M-row shuffle of meters. The bigger meters gets, the more valuable the broadcast becomes for avoiding the shuffle.
Neither — at Mid scale the engineer should switch to a different join algorithm entirely (ShuffleHashJoin); both plans become inefficient and require explicit rewriting.
Plan A and Plan B perform identically at 12M scale because AQE adapts both at runtime to the optimal strategy. Plan choice does not matter once AQE is enabled cluster-wide.
fields.correctAnswer: Plan B remains preferred because the substations table is still tiny; broadcasting it eliminates the 12M-row shuffle of meters. The bigger meters gets, the more valuable the broadcast becomes for avoiding the shuffle.
fields.rationale: Substations is reference data — it does not grow with meter count. At 12M meters the meters shuffle in Plan A would be 24× larger than at Junior scale; broadcasting the still-tiny substations becomes even more valuable. The general rule: broadcast scales with the SMALL side, not the large side. AQE will often automatically convert SortMergeJoin to BroadcastHashJoin at runtime if it detects the small side is broadcastable, but explicit hints make the intention visible in the plan.
fields.distractorRationale:
Option A: Reverses the scaling direction; bigger meters means MORE benefit from broadcast, not less.

Option C: Suggests a different join algorithm without justification; ShuffleHashJoin is rarely the right choice.

Option D: Treats AQE as a substitute for choosing the right join. AQE helps but explicit hints remain useful.

tasks.pssReference: PSI1 lessons 3, 8 (Reading Physical Plans, AQE Overview), PSI3 (Join Performance and Shuffle Optimization).
